authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 01): introduce Ticket as a domain entity behind a repository boundary. Why was an active-record style model rejected?

choices.text: It would couple the business terms of Ticket to Express and storage infrastructure.
Active-record models cannot hold comments and audit events.
The in-memory repository cannot persist active-record objects.
Active records make DTOs unnecessary, so the API shape could not evolve.

authored.explanation: Keep Domain free of Express and storage details; active-record couples business terms to infrastructure (NOTES.md:10).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 02): make ticket status transitions a real backend feature that stays testable. Where does the transition behaviour live?

choices.text: In TicketService; controllers stay thin and delegate to it.
In TicketsController, next to the route that receives the request.
In the in-memory repository's save method.
In the React page that changes the status dropdown.

authored.explanation: Status transition behavior goes in a service; controller-level business logic was rejected as hard to test (NOTES.md:7,10).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 04): make bad input and failures predictable across the API. Which design choice delivers a consistent error shape?

choices.text: Errors are centralized in global error middleware, with validation at the HTTP boundary.
Each controller writes its own try/catch and formats its own error response.
Services re-validate every field so the HTTP layer can stay permissive.
A full form library on the frontend guarantees no invalid request reaches the API.

authored.explanation: Ad hoc try/catch responses were rejected because they drift by controller; validate at the HTTP boundary (NOTES.md:10-11).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 05): record what happened during an incident. How are incident timeline events treated, and why?

choices.text: Append-only, because operational history should be preserved.
Editable in place, so responders can correct typos in earlier entries.
Stored inside each linked Ticket's comments to avoid a second collection.
Deleted when the incident is resolved to keep the list short.

authored.explanation: Treat timeline events as append-only because operational history should be preserved (NOTES.md:12).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 06): protect sensitive operations by role. What is the actual security control?

choices.text: Role middleware on the sensitive backend endpoints.
Hiding the buttons in role-aware navigation.
The demo token stored in localStorage.
The protected route wrapper in the React router.

authored.explanation: Server-side authorization is the actual control; role-aware UI is not the source of truth (NOTES.md:10,12).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 08): make ticket status changes feel instant under latency. Where were optimistic updates allowed?

choices.text: Only where the rollback story is simple.
On every mutation, since the query cache can always refetch.
Nowhere; the snapshot installs TanStack Query to handle it.
Only on login, so the user sees the dashboard sooner.

authored.explanation: Add optimistic updates only where the rollback story is simple; a local teaching cache was used instead of TanStack Query (NOTES.md:10-11).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 10): make runtime configuration auditable. Which approach does the snapshot take?

choices.text: Load config once at startup instead of scattered process.env reads.
Read process.env at each call site so values can change at runtime.
Store configuration in the in-memory repository.
Pass configuration through the correlation ID header.

authored.explanation: Scattered process.env reads were rejected because they are hard to audit (NOTES.md:10).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 11): predict the cost of the BEFORE version. GET /api/incidents returns five incidents, each linking three tickets. How many repository calls does the before code make?

choices.text: 1 incident list call plus 15 ticket lookups
1 incident list call plus 1 batched ticket lookup
1 incident list call plus 5 ticket lookups
A single joined call for incidents and tickets

authored.explanation: Five incidents with three linked tickets each created fifteen ticket repository calls after the incident query (performance-incident-list.md:5,11).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 12): keep large list endpoints safe. Why is the page size capped on the server even though the UI dropdown only offers safe values?

choices.text: The UI cannot be trusted to protect the database.
The dropdown values are not serialised into the query string.
Express rejects query strings above 100 characters.
Logs are read-only, so they need a different cap than tickets.

authored.explanation: Use bounded pagination on the server because the UI cannot be trusted to protect the database (NOTES.md:10).

authored.prompt: Goal (snapshot 13): defend against password guessing. Why is login rate-limited separately from normal API traffic?

choices.text: Password guessing has a different risk profile from ordinary API use.
Normal API traffic is already limited by the ErrorBoundary.
Login is the only route without security headers.
A shared limiter would log the user out after token expiry.

authored.explanation: Rate-limit login separately because password guessing has a different risk profile (NOTES.md:10).
